prompt.context: Your client is a non-profit art museum -- let's call it the Museum of Fine Arts, or MFA -- in a large, metropolitan city on the East Coast with the largest collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist works in North America. Last year, it attracted over 1 million visitors and acquired new pieces through Sotheby's, a major auction house. Despite these successes, the MFA's revenue stream has been declining for the last two years, which is unusual when compared to similar art museums. The current director, Matthew, has approached you for advice.
prompt.question: What are sources of revenue for the MFA and why might revenue have decreased?

clarifying_info.a: Members pay an annual fee for access to the galleries, exhibitions, and events.

clarifying_info.q: Have ticket prices or membership prices changed?
How many members does the MFA have?
clarifying_info.a: The MFA expects to keep a steady base of 11,500 members, which you can round to 12,000, over the next few years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the retention rate from year 1 to year 2?
clarifying_info.a: The probability that a member continues from year 1 to year 2 is 80%, and from year 2 to year 3 and beyond is 50%.

exhibits.title: Ticket Sales and Membership Enrollment
exhibits.shows: A table showing tickets and memberships sold (thousands) and revenue from ticket sales and membership fees ($M) for years 2013, 2014, and 2015

exhibits.title: Survey Results on Price Sensitivity
exhibits.shows: A demand curve chart showing ticket price on the x-axis ($0 to $28) and percentage of surveyed patrons willing to buy on the y-axis (0% to 100%)

exhibits.title: Member Lifetime Value
exhibits.shows: A diagram showing average revenue generated per member per year broken into three periods: Year 1, Year 2, and Year 3 and beyond

framework: Revenue sources for a non-profit museum: (1) Sales -- tickets, memberships, ancillary (gift shop, audio tours); (2) Individual giving -- donor base size, frequency of donation, average donation size; (3) Endowment -- annual distribution percentage, rate of return; (4) Grants -- government and private foundations
To diagnose the decline, assess what has changed recently across each revenue stream; look for shifts in patron mix, donor behavior, endowment performance, or grant availability
Context-specific hypotheses are stronger than generic ones (e.g., a competing cause edging out arts donations, tourists replacing local members)

questions.prompt: Part 2: Given Exhibit A, what do you notice about ticket sales and membership enrollment?
questions.guidance: Even though combined tickets and memberships sold increased from 890k to 1,021k (2013-2015), revenue fell from $13.0M to $13.2M (barely flat, then declined). Since prices held constant, this means the mix shifted: more lower-priced tickets and fewer higher-priced memberships. Candidate should ask about prices; when told they are unchanged, conclude that memberships carry a higher price than tickets, and the revenue decline is driven by declining membership enrollment despite rising ticket sales. Candidate should then brainstorm why memberships declined while ticket sales rose.

questions.prompt: Part 2 brainstorm: Why might membership enrollment have declined while ticket sales increased?
questions.guidance: Changing patron composition by geography (more out-of-town tourists buy tickets not memberships); changing age composition (younger visitors volunteer rather than pay memberships); price sensitivity (membership fees are larger one-time outlays, more sensitive to income changes); museum less effective at attracting or retaining members (changed benefits, missed target exhibitions)

questions.prompt: Part 3: Using Exhibit B, what ticket price do you recommend to maximize revenue?
questions.guidance: Treat the demand curve as price x quantity. Use 100 as a baseline of potential patrons (simplifying assumption) or reference ~1M ticket buyers from Exhibit A. Calculate revenue at each price point and select the maximum. Candidate should also name the mission tradeoff: raising prices reduces access to price-sensitive patrons, which conflicts with the MFA's non-profit mission of broadening art access.

math.setup: Revenue = ticket price x (% willing to buy x total potential patrons). Using 100 baseline patrons:
steps: Impact quantification: current revenue = 1M buyers x $12 = $12.0M; new revenue = 800k buyers (60% of ~1.33M total population, since 75% = 1M implies total = 1.33M, so 60% = 800k) x $16 = $12.8M; additional revenue = ~$800k
math.answer: Recommend raising ticket price from $12 to $16, generating approximately $800k in additional annual revenue

questions.prompt: Part 4a: Using Exhibit C plus retention data, what is the average expected lifetime revenue per member?
questions.guidance: Exhibit C shows average revenue per year but does not account for retention. Candidate should ask for retention rates. Apply probabilities cumulatively: Year 1 is certain (100%), Year 2 requires surviving to year 2 (80%), Year 3+ requires surviving to year 2 (80%) AND then to year 3 (50%). Each period contributes $80 in expected revenue, summing to $240 total. Strong candidate notes that $240 excludes member acquisition cost and that retention rate is a lever to manage.

math.setup: Expected revenue per member = sum of (revenue per period x cumulative probability of reaching that period)
math.answer: Average expected lifetime revenue per member = $240

questions.prompt: Part 4b: The MFA is considering spending $1.2M upfront to improve membership benefits, expecting to raise the year-2-to-year-3 retention rate. Is this worth it?
questions.guidance: Candidate should find the breakeven retention rate (year 2 to year 3) at which incremental revenue = $1.2M. Divide the cost by the member base to get per-member threshold, then work backwards through the probability math. The breakeven retention rate exceeds 100%, which is impossible, so the initiative is not worth it. Bonus: candidate notes that improved membership could cannibalize ticket sales, adding another reason to reject the initiative. Suggest alternative revenue ideas (event rentals, targeted giving campaigns, summer programs).

math.setup: Find retention rate x (year 2 to year 3+) such that incremental revenue per member x 12,000 members = $1.2M
steps: $1.2M / 12,000 members = $100 incremental revenue needed per member in year 3 and beyond
Incremental revenue per member from raising retention rate: 80% (year-1-to-2 retention) x x (incremental retention rate year-2-to-3) x $200 (year 3+ avg revenue) = $100
Breakeven retention rate from year 2 to year 3 = 50% (current) + 62.5% (required increase) = 112.5%
math.answer: Breakeven retention rate would need to be 112.5% -- impossible. The $1.2M initiative cannot pay for itself; do not pursue.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might membership enrollment have declined while ticket sales increased?

categories.name: Patron composition by geography
ideas: Out-of-town tourists are more likely to buy single tickets than annual memberships
Visitor base has been skewing toward tourists who have no reason to hold annual memberships

categories.name: Patron composition by age
ideas: Younger visitors tend to support museums through volunteering rather than paid memberships
MFA's support base is becoming younger and less likely to enroll in memberships

categories.name: Price sensitivity
ideas: Membership fees are a larger upfront outlay and thus more sensitive to drops in disposable income
In an economic downturn, patrons may downgrade from memberships to single tickets

categories.name: Membership program effectiveness
ideas: Museum less effective at attracting new members (marketing, outreach)
Museum less effective at retaining existing members (benefits changed, special exhibitions missed the target)
Competing art institutions or causes pulling away potential members

recommendation: Raise adult ticket price from $12 to $16 to capture approximately $800k in additional annual revenue
Do not invest the $1.2M in the proposed membership benefits revamp; the required retention improvement exceeds 100% and cannot pay back the investment
risks: Raising ticket price is at odds with MFA's non-profit mission to increase public access to art; price-sensitive segments (schools, lower-income patrons) may be priced out
Improved membership benefits could cannibalize ticket sales, reducing net revenue gain
Revenue from endowment, grants, and individual giving may be declining independently and warrant separate investigation
next_steps: Analyze ticket price sensitivity by patron segment (e.g., schools, senior citizens) to design tiered pricing that balances revenue with mission
Explore alternative revenue levers: renting gallery space for corporate events, targeted individual giving campaigns for new donor segments, summer programs for students
Investigate root causes of membership decline in more depth (patron surveys, competitor benchmarking) before abandoning membership initiatives entirely
Review endowment allocation and grant pipeline to assess whether non-ticket revenue streams are also under pressure
